slides.headline:
A 2,000-won bottle
cost a stall three days.
slides.subline: Korea spent 2026 rewriting what a market stall may charge you. Here is what actually changed

slides.label: Tourism complaints filed in Korea in the first seven months of 2026 — already more than the 1,744 logged in all of 2025, and the highest figure on record. Shopping disputes over price and service were the second-largest category, at 376
slides.note: Source: Korea Tourism Organization / Korea Tourism Data Lab, reported by The Korea Herald, 6 September 2026. Counted from the Tourist Complaint Center website and the 1330 hotline · Checked 26 September 2026

items.t: A first offence now costs a lodging five days
items.d: From 4 August 2026, accommodation that fails to post a price list or charges more than it posted is suspended for five days on the first violation, ten on the second, twenty on the third. The first used to be a warning

items.t: Overcharging taxi drivers lose 30 days, immediately
items.d: Same decree, no warning stage. Sixty days for a second offence; the licence is revoked on a third

items.t: Gwangjang's street stalls have registered names
items.d: Jongno-gu started a street-vendor real-name system in June 2026. Stalls run on demerit points, and a permit can be revoked past 120
Seoul inspected 159 restaurants and 109 food stalls at Gwangjang in May–June 2026 and left a standing monitoring system behind it

slides.title:
Why it came down
to a water bottle.
slides.body:
In April 2026 a Myanmar-born YouTuber living in Korea filmed paying 2,000 won for a 500ml bottle of water at a Gwangjang Market stall. Most stalls there charge 1,000; three charged 2,000. The vendors' association suspended that stall for three days, ruled that water served in a cup is free, and told anyone selling bottled water to put the price on the menu.

It was not the first. In November 2025 a video with more than 16 million views showed a vendor charging 10,000 won for a dish listed at 8,000, and that stall was suspended for ten days. The complaints before it were about portions rather than sticker prices — a roughly 15-dollar assorted-pancake platter of about ten small pieces in late 2024 — which is why Gwangjang's fix was a fixed-quantity labelling system.

slides.title:
If you're eating
at a market

items.t: The posted price is the whole price
items.d: A 2013 revision of the Food Sanitation Act requires restaurant menu prices to be final — tax and service included, nothing added at the end. There is no tipping to budget for

items.t: Ask what a set costs and what is in it
items.d: The disputes that actually escalated were about portion size and add-ons, not the number on the board. Settle both before you sit down

items.t: Water in a cup should not be charged for
items.d: That is the Gwangjang vendors' association's own April 2026 ruling. A bottle can be sold, but the price has to be on the menu

items.t: 1330 takes the complaint in your language
items.d: The Korea Travel Hotline is free and multilingual, and it is one of the two channels the record complaint numbers are counted from

slides.text:
This is research, not a personal visit.
Every figure here comes from a published source, checked on 26 September 2026.
slides.by: Two things this post is not saying. Korean markets are not a scam: the record complaint count covers the whole tourism industry, and lodging — not food — is its largest single category at 500. And the tightened penalties in the 4 August decree apply to accommodation and taxis. The stall rules at Gwangjang are a Jongno-gu and merchants'-association system, not a national law, so what binds one stall may not bind the next market you walk into.

caption:
A 2,000-won bottle of water got a Gwangjang Market stall suspended for three days this April. That sounds like a small story. It is actually the clearest signal of what changed in Korea in 2026.

Tourism complaints hit a record: 1,753 in the first seven months of the year, already more than the 1,744 filed in all of 2025, according to Korea Tourism Organization figures. The government's answer arrived on 4 August. Accommodation that doesn't post a price list, or charges more than it posted, is now suspended for five days on a first offence instead of warned. A taxi driver caught overcharging loses the licence for 30 days on the first offence, 60 on the second, permanently on the third.

At Gwangjang specifically: Jongno-gu started a street-vendor real-name system in June, Seoul inspected 159 restaurants and 109 stalls in May and June, and mystery shoppers — Korean and foreign — are still working the aisles.

What this means when you're standing at a stall in Seoul: the posted price is the whole price. A 2013 revision of the Food Sanitation Act requires menu prices to include tax and service, and there is no tipping on top. Ask what a set costs and what's in it before you sit down, because the fights that escalated were about portions, not the number on the board. Water in a cup is free. And if something goes wrong, 1330 takes the complaint in English.

Korean markets are not a scam — lodging, not food, is the biggest complaint category. But the rules got sharper this year, and they work better if you know them. Sources in the last slide.
